q: Which translator converts an entire high-level program into machine code before it is run?
x: A compiler translates the whole source program at once and produces an executable. An interpreter translates and runs one statement at a time, and an assembler translates only assembly language.
Both operands are int, so C performs integer division and discards the fractional part: 17 ÷ 5 = 3. The value 3.4 would need at least one float operand.
'A' has ASCII code 65, so c + 2 is 67. With %c the code 67 prints as the letter C and with %d it prints as the number 67.

q: Which of the following is true about an interpreter?
o: It produces a separate executable file for the whole program
It is a hardware device that is fitted on the motherboard
It translates only assembly language into machine code
It translates and executes the program one statement at a time
x: An interpreter reads, translates and runs each statement in turn, so errors appear when that line is reached. A compiler is the one that produces a separate executable.

q:
What is the output of the following code?
```
printf("%d", 17 % 5);
```
x: The % operator gives the remainder: 17 = 3 × 5 + 2, so the result is 2. The quotient is 3, which is a different operation.

q: Which function is normally used to read input from the keyboard in C?
x: scanf reads formatted input from the keyboard. printf is for output.

q: Which header file must be included to use printf() in C?
x: printf and scanf are declared in stdio.h, the standard input/output header. math.h has functions such as sqrt and string.h has string functions.
Post-increment gives y the old value 5 first and then raises x to 6. So x = 6 and y = 5; the output "6 6" would be right for ++x.

q: Which format specifier prints a float value in printf()?
x: %f is for real numbers. %d is for int, %c is for one character and %s is for a string.

q: In a C program, execution starts from the function:
x: Every C program begins running at main(). The other names have no special meaning.
Pre-increment raises x to 10 before it is used, so y = 10 + 1 = 11. The value of x is already 10 when printed.

q:
What is the output of the following code?
```
printf("%d %d %d", 5 > 3 && 2 > 4, 5 > 3 || 2 > 4, !(5 > 3));
```
x: True && false is 0, true || false is 1 and !true is 0. In C a true comparison has the value 1.

q:
What is the output of the following code?
```
printf("%d", 2 + 3 * 4 - 6 / 2);
```
x: Multiplication and division come first: 3 × 4 = 12 and 6 ÷ 2 = 3, so 2 + 12 − 3 = 11. Working strictly left to right would wrongly give 7.

q:
What is the output of the following code?
```
printf("%d", 100 / 10 * 5);
```
x: Operators of equal precedence are evaluated left to right: 100 / 10 = 10 and then 10 × 5 = 50. The answer 2 would need brackets around 10 * 5.
Left to right: 10 / 4 = 2 in integer division, then 2 × 2 = 4. The value 5 would come from doing the multiplication first.
10 / 4 is evaluated first as an integer division giving 2, and only then stored as 2.0 in the float. Writing 10.0 / 4 would give 2.5.

q: Which of the following is a valid variable name in C?
x: An identifier may contain letters, digits and underscores but must not start with a digit or contain spaces. float is a reserved keyword, so it cannot be used either.

q: Which data type is used to store a number with a fractional part?
x: float stores real numbers such as 3.75. int holds whole numbers, char holds a single character and void means no value.

q: Which operator is used in C to test whether two values are equal?
x: The double equals sign compares values, while a single = assigns a value. Writing = inside an if condition is a classic bug.

q: Which of the following is a reserved word (keyword) in C?
x: while is a keyword of the language. print, integer and loop are not keywords of C.

q: What is the ASCII code of 'D', if the ASCII code of 'A' is 65?
x: The letters follow one another in order: A = 65, B = 66, C = 67, D = 68. The value 67 belongs to C.
x becomes 7 − 2 = 5 and then 5 × 3 = 15. The statements run one after another and not in one combined formula.

q: Every preprocessor directive in a C program, such as include or define, starts with which symbol?
x: Preprocessor directives begin with # (for example `#include` and `#define`) and are handled before compilation. & is the address-of operator.

q: In which order does a C program pass through these stages before it runs?
x: The preprocessor first handles the # directives, the compiler then makes object code, the linker joins it with library code into an executable, and the loader puts that into memory. Linking cannot come before there is object code to link.

q: What does the compiler produce when it translates a C source file without errors?
o: A header file that other programs can include
An object file of machine code that still has to be linked
The source file with all # directives replaced
The program's output on the screen
x: The compiler turns the source into object code; the linker then adds the library code (such as printf's) to make the executable. Replacing # directives is the preprocessor's job.

q: A program compiles without any error, but no executable file is made because the body of a function it calls cannot be found in any file or library. Which program reports this error?
x: Joining the program's object code with the code of the functions it calls is the linker's job, so a missing function body is a linking error. The compiler only checks the program's own statements.

DOUBLE(3) * 2 becomes ((3)+(3)) * 2 = 6 * 2 = 12. Without the outer brackets it would be 3+3*2 = 9.
M * 2 is replaced by N+1 * 2 and then by 4+1 * 2; multiplication comes first, so 4 + 2 = 6. The answer 10 assumes (4+1) * 2, but the macro has no brackets.
The preprocessor does not replace names inside a string literal, so the text MAX = stays as it is, while the second MAX becomes 10 and is printed by %d.

It compiles but gives an error only when it runs
x: The semicolon becomes part of the macro, so the line turns into printf("%d", 10; * 2); which is a syntax error found at compile time. Directives must not end with a semicolon.
Everything between /* and */ is a comment and is ignored, so x stays 5 and then becomes 6. The answer 11 wrongly runs the commented line.

q: What is the difference between `#include <file.h>` and `#include "file.h"`?
o: Angle brackets search the standard include folder; quotes look in the program's own folder first
Quotes search the standard include folder; angle brackets look in the program's own folder first
Quotes may be used only for standard library headers
There is no difference; both search exactly the same places
x: Angle brackets are used for standard headers such as stdio.h, which live in the compiler's include folder. Quotes are used for the programmer's own header files, which are searched for in the current folder first.

q: In C, which symbol marks the end of a statement such as `x = 5`?
x: Every C statement ends with a semicolon. A comma separates items in one statement, for example in a declaration list.

o: It gives an error only when it runs
x: C is case-sensitive, so Total and total are different names, and Total was never declared; the compiler reports an undeclared identifier. The program never gets far enough to print anything.

q: A programmer forgets the semicolon at the end of a statement. What kind of error is this?
x: Breaking the grammar rules of the language is a syntax error, and the compiler reports it. A logical error does not break any rule; it only gives a wrong result.
Division is done before addition: b / 2 = 4, then 4 + 4 = 8 instead of the average 6. The program compiles and runs, so this is a logical error; (a + b) / 2 would be correct.

q: What does an IDE used for C programming provide?
o: Only a faster processor for running programs
A printed list of all C keywords
An editor, compiler, linker and debugger in one program
A network connection between two computers
x: An Integrated Development Environment brings the tools for writing, translating, linking and debugging a program into one place. It is software, not hardware.

q: Which of these happens during preprocessing, before the compiler starts?
o: Each #include line is replaced by the contents of that header file
Syntax errors such as a missing semicolon are reported
Object code is joined with library code
The executable file is copied into memory
x: The preprocessor handles the # directives, for example inserting header files and replacing macros. Reporting syntax errors is the compiler's work and joining code is the linker's.

q: The statement `area = PI * r * r;` must use 3.14 for PI. Which line, written at the top of the program, makes it compile correctly?
x: #define is written as name, space, replacement text, with no = and no semicolon. With = the statement becomes area = = 3.14 * r * r; with the semicolon it becomes area = 3.14; * r * r, and without # the line is not a directive at all.
return 0; ends main, and so the program, after One is printed; the second printf is never reached. OneTwo would need the return statement at the end.

q: Which program copies an executable file into main memory so that it can run?
x: The loader places the executable in memory and starts it. The linker only makes the executable file; it does not run it.

q: In a program written as `int main()`, what does `return 0;` at the end of main tell the operating system?
o: That the program must run again
That an error occurred at line 0
x: The value returned by main is passed to the operating system, and 0 means successful completion. Nothing is printed by return.

q: After a C program has been compiled and linked, which file can the operating system run directly?
x: Linking produces the executable file, which is complete machine code ready to load and run. The object file is machine code too, but the library code it needs is not yet joined to it.

q: Which statement about the main() function is correct?
o: A C program may have several main functions
main must be the last function written in the file
It may be written Main, since C ignores capital letters
A C program must have exactly one main function
x: Execution starts at main, so a program has one and only one main function. C is case-sensitive, so Main would be a different name.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%.1f", (float)7 / 2);
```
x: The cast applies to 7 first, making it 7.0, so the division is done in floating point: 7.0 / 2 = 3.5. The value 3.0 would come from (float)(7 / 2).

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%.1f", 7 / 2 * 2.0);
```
x: Left to right: 7 / 2 is integer division giving 3, then 3 * 2.0 = 6.0. The value 7.0 assumes the fractional part of 3.5 is kept.
Relational operators work left to right: 1 < 5 is true and gives 1, then 1 < 3 is also true, giving 1. It does not test whether a lies between 1 and 3, which would be false.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%d", !0 + 3 * 2);
```
x: ! has the highest precedence here, so !0 is 1; then 3 * 2 = 6 and 1 + 6 = 7. The answer 0 wrongly applies ! to the whole expression.
Assignment works right to left, so b = 4 first and then a = 4. a += b makes a 8 and leaves b at 4.

q: Which keyword makes a variable's value fixed, so that the program cannot change it after it is given a value?
x: A variable declared with const, such as const int N = 5;, cannot be assigned again. unsigned only stops it from holding negative values.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%d", 'a' - 'A');
```
x: Characters are stored as ASCII codes: 'a' is 97 and 'A' is 65, so the difference is 32. It is not 0, because small and capital letters have different codes.

q: How many of these are valid identifiers in C: `_rate`, `Total2`, `2ndValue`, `net pay`, `auto`?
x: _rate and Total2 are valid, since an identifier may start with a letter or underscore. 2ndValue starts with a digit, net pay has a space and auto is a C keyword.
When a real value is stored in an int, the fractional part is dropped, not rounded, so x is 7. The value 8 assumes rounding.

q: Which of these is NOT a keyword in C?
x: main is the name of a function (an identifier), not a reserved word. int, return and char are keywords.

q: Which format specifier prints an int in hexadecimal?
x: %x prints an integer in base 16. %o prints it in octal (base 8) and %d in decimal.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%o %x", 10, 255);
```
x: 10 in octal is 12 (1 × 8 + 2) and 255 in hexadecimal is ff (15 × 16 + 15). The output a 377 swaps the two specifiers.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%.2f", 3.14159);
```
x: %.2f prints two digits after the decimal point; the third digit is 1, so 3.14159 rounds to 3.14. 3.15 would need the third digit to be 5 or more.
%f without a precision prints six digits after the decimal point. To print 2.5 you would write %.1f.

q:
How many spaces are printed before the digit 3?
```
printf("%6.2f", 3.14159);
```
x: %6.2f prints 3.14 (4 characters: 3, the point, 1, 4) in a field 6 wide, so 2 spaces are added on the left. The 6 counts the whole field, not just the digits after the point.

q:
How many spaces are printed between the first | and the 4?
```
printf("|%5d|", 42);
```
x: %5d prints 42 right-aligned in 5 places, so 3 spaces come before it. The 5 is the total width, not the number of spaces.

q:
How many spaces are printed between 7 and 8?
```
printf("%-4d%d", 7, 8);
```
x: The minus sign left-aligns 7 in a field 4 wide, so 3 spaces follow it before 8 is printed. Without the minus sign the spaces would come before 7.

q:
How many spaces does this statement print in total?
```
printf("%3d%3d", 7, 45);
```
x: 7 gets 2 spaces before it to fill 3 places, and 45 gets 1 space, giving 2 + 1 = 3 spaces. The answer 6 adds both widths without taking the digits away.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%d%%", 50);
```
x: Inside a format string %% prints one % sign, so the output is 50%. A single % on its own would start a new format specifier.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%.3s", "Pakistan");
```
x: With %s, the precision .3 limits the output to the first 3 characters of the string. It takes characters from the start, not the end.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("Ali\\Khan");
```
x: The escape sequence \\ prints a single backslash, so the output is Ali\Khan. Two backslashes are written in the code because one alone starts an escape sequence.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("He said \"Hi\"");
```
x: \" is the escape sequence for a double quote inside a string, so both quotes around Hi are printed and the backslashes are not. The outer quotes of the string are never printed.

q:
How many lines of output does this statement produce?
```
printf("A\nB\n\nC");
```
x: A is on line 1, the first \n moves to line 2 for B, the next \n ends that line, the third gives an empty line 3, and C is on line 4. The answer 3 forgets the empty line.

q: What does the escape sequence `\a` produce when it is printed?
x: \a is the alert (bell) character. A backspace is \b, a new line \n and a tab \t.

q: In `scanf("%d", &x);`, why is the & sign written before x?
o: It gives scanf the address of x, so the value read can be stored in x
It joins x to the format string
It prints the value of x after reading
x: & is the address-of operator; scanf needs the memory address of x to put the input there. printf does not need & because it only reads the value.

q: A variable is declared as `double d;`. Which format specifier is used in scanf to read a value into it?
x: %lf reads a double. %ld reads a long int and %d an int, so they cannot read a real value correctly.

o: Hello on one line, World on the next
x: printf does not add a space or a new line by itself; the second string is printed right after the first. A new line needs \n in the format string.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%05d", 42);
```
x: The 0 flag fills the 5-wide field with leading zeros instead of spaces, giving 00042. The zeros are added on the left, not the right.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%.1f", 2.46);
```
x: %.1f keeps one decimal place and rounds: the next digit is 6, so 2.46 becomes 2.5. The value 2.4 would mean the digits are cut off rather than rounded.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%d + %d = %d", 4, 3, 4 * 3);
```
x: The + and = in the format string are printed as plain text, while the three %d are replaced by 4, 3 and the value of 4 * 3 = 12. printf does not work out the sum written in its text.
